title: Poverty in India
tagline: The poverty line and its calorie basis, absolute and relative poverty, and the causes that keep either one in place.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: Poverty is the first of the major problems the syllabus assigns to the Indian economy, and it is studied in a strict three-part order: how poverty is measured, in what two senses it exists, and why it persists. The measurement question comes first because poverty without a line is only a sentiment — the syllabus’s answer is the poverty line built on calorie intake, the physical basis that turns an idea into a countable threshold. The two senses follow: absolute poverty is falling below that minimum of food and basic needs, while relative poverty is the distance between groups inside the same society, which exists wherever anyone has much less than others even if no one is starving. The causes come last and carry the analytical weight — five or more are prescribed, each of them a mechanism rather than an adjective: income without work, more mouths than livelihoods, an unequal slice of a growing pie, schooling that never happened, and prices rising faster than earnings. The chapter’s discipline is to keep measurement, description and explanation in their own compartments, because examinations ask for each separately.

learningOutcomes: Explain poverty and the concept of the poverty line, including its calorie basis.
Distinguish absolute from relative poverty with examples.
State and explain at least five causes of poverty.
Apply the poverty line and the two senses of poverty to concrete households.
Relate poverty to the employment problem it is paired with in the syllabus.

learn.title: Poverty and the poverty line: a threshold built on calories

blocks.text: Poverty is the condition of not having the income required to meet the basic necessities of life — adequate food, clothing, shelter, education and health. The definition is honest but unusable on its own: to count the poor, the word “basic” has to be converted into a threshold, and that threshold is the poverty line. The syllabus’s prescribed basis is calorie intake, and the logic is physical before it is economic. A working person needs a minimum energy — roughly 2400 calories a day in a rural area and 2100 in an urban area in the convention usually taught — because rural work burns more energy and urban food is more calorie-dense. Below that intake a person weakens, falls ill and earns less, which makes the calorie norm not a lifestyle opinion but the floor beneath earning capacity. The line is then built by asking what income buys that diet for a household, and families whose income falls short of that expenditure are counted as being below the line — the headcount of the poor. Two properties matter for exam answers. The line is a minimum: it certifies deprivation of necessities, not unhappiness and not inequality. And it is absolute by construction: it does not move when the rich grow richer, so it can show poverty falling as incomes rise while saying nothing about the distance between the top and the bottom — which is precisely why the syllabus teaches a second sense of poverty alongside it.

learn.title: Absolute and relative poverty: two senses, two questions

blocks.text: Absolute poverty answers the question “can this household meet minimum needs?” — it is the condition of falling below the subsistence floor of food, clothing and shelter, and it is what the poverty line measures. Its examples are the ones the line’s arithmetic produces: a landless labourer’s family whose earnings never reach the calorie-norm expenditure, a daily-wage household eating two meals of thin food because the third costs a day’s wage, a family in a single room without safe water sharing it with illness. Relative poverty answers a different question — “how far below others does this household stand?” — and it is the gap between groups within the same society. A worker who eats adequately yet cannot match the schooling, clothing or housing of families in the same town is relatively poor; discrimination that pays one group less for the same work, or a region left behind while the rest of the country grows, creates relative poverty even when no one is below the calorie norm. The two senses are not rivals but a measurement pair. Absolute poverty can be counted with a line and tracked over time, which makes it the target of food security and wage-employment programmes. Relative poverty cannot be abolished by raising everyone above a floor — it disappears only when the distance closes, which is a question of distribution rather than of subsistence. An economy can therefore report absolute poverty falling while relative poverty widens, and both statements would be true of the same decade.

items: Absolute poverty: below the minimum — measured by the calorie-based line, remedied by raising incomes to the floor.
Absolute examples: landless labourer below the norm, thin meals, a family with neither shelter nor safe water.
Relative poverty: the gap within society — inadequate schooling, housing or status compared with neighbours.
Relative examples: equal work paid unequally across groups; a region stagnant while the country grows.
Both can move independently: the floor can rise while the distance widens, and vice versa.

blocks.text: The syllabus asks for any five causes, and each of the standard five is a mechanism that reproduces itself. Low income and unemployment sit at the centre: where work is casual, seasonal or absent, household earnings never accumulate beyond the next meal, so there is no surplus for education, insurance or assets — poverty as the arithmetic of no reliable wage. Rapid population growth works on the denominator: more mouths divide the same income, and when new workers enter the labour market faster than jobs are created, unemployment and low wages are the predictable result. Unequal distribution of income and wealth operates even while the economy grows: if the gains concentrate in a few regions, sectors and households, national income can rise with the number below the line unchanged — the pie grows and the slice does not. Illiteracy and lack of education or training close the loop from the other end: without skills, workers are confined to the lowest-paid work with no route upward, and their children repeat the same confinement because school fees and lost child wages put education out of reach. Rising prices finish the mechanism set: inflation in food, fuel and rent erodes the real value of fixed and casual incomes, so a household can earn nominally the same and afford less each year — and the poor, who spend almost everything on essentials, absorb price rises most completely. The syllabus’s “any five” rewards precision: each cause stated as a causal chain — condition, mechanism, consequence — rather than as a heading in a list.

items.meaning: Earnings too small or too irregular to clear the subsistence floor.
items.context: The central cause: without a reliable wage nothing else in the list can be fixed.

items.meaning: More earners-to-support than the household income can carry, and entrants outpacing job creation.
items.context: Population growth divides income and swells the job-seeker queue together.

items.meaning: Growth whose gains concentrate in fewer hands and regions.
items.context: Distribution decides whether rising national income reaches the bottom.

items.meaning: Absence of the schooling and skills that unlock higher-paid work.
items.context: Illiteracy reproduces poverty across generations through the same mechanism.

items.meaning: Prices rising faster than the incomes of the poor.
items.context: The poor spend nearly all income on essentials, so price rises hit them first and hardest.

learn.title: Reading poverty in practice: what the line shows and what it leaves to other senses

blocks.text: Applied to real households, the line is most useful when its boundaries are understood rather than hidden. A farming family with land but a failed monsoon may fall below the line in one year and above it in the next — poverty measured annually is a moving condition, which is why vulnerability, the risk of falling below, is part of the practical picture even though the line counts only those who have fallen. A household just above the line is not comfortable: one illness, one funeral, one school fee can push it down, since it has no savings buffer — the line marks a cliff rather than a slope. And the two senses answer different policy questions on the same street: a family below the calorie norm needs food and income support urgently, while a family above the norm whose children attend no school is not below the absolute line yet is denied mobility — relative poverty’s territory, treated by public education and health rather than by food alone. The examiner’s version of this discipline is a comparison answer: state what the calorie line certifies (minimum needs), what it cannot see (distance between groups, near-poor vulnerability), and therefore which tool addresses which — income and food programmes for absolute poverty, universal services and progressive distribution for relative. Measurement is not an academic preliminary to the problem; it decides which households are counted, which programmes are funded and which poverty goes officially unseen.

items.text: A daily-wage family earns just above the calorie-implied expenditure in a good month and well below it when work dries up for three weeks.
items.note: Vulnerability around the line: counted as non-poor in one month, poor in the next.

items.text: Two neighbouring households eat adequately; one’s children finish school, the other’s do not.
items.note: Relative poverty without absolute poverty — mobility denied while the calorie norm is met.

keyPoints: Poverty is inability to meet basic necessities; counting it requires a threshold — the poverty line.
The prescribed basis is calorie intake: about 2400 kcal rural and 2100 kcal urban per person per day.
The calorie norm is physical first: below it, earning capacity itself falls.
The line is absolute — it certifies minimum deprivation, not inequality.
Absolute poverty: below the minimum; relative poverty: the gap between groups in the same society.
Both senses can move independently — the floor can rise while the distance widens.
Five causes, each a chain: low income and unemployment; population growth; unequal distribution; illiteracy; inflation erosion.
Distribution decides whether national growth reaches the bottom at all.
The poor spend almost all income on essentials, so price rises hit them disproportionately.
Households just above the line are vulnerable — the line is a cliff, not a slope.
Policy follows measurement: food and income tools for absolute poverty, universal services and distribution for relative.
examFocus: Define poverty, then immediately introduce the line — measurement first, as the syllabus orders it.
Explain the calorie basis as physical logic: floor beneath earning capacity, not a lifestyle figure.
Give the rural and urban calorie norms in the standard convention and say they are per person per day.
Distinguish absolute and relative with a matched pair of examples — that pairing earns the mark.
Causes must be chains: condition → mechanism → consequence, at least five of them.
State growth and distribution separately: a rising pie with an unchanged slice is unequal distribution, not absence of growth.
Handle the near-poor explicitly when asked to apply the line — vulnerability is where application marks live.
Close measurement answers by linking each sense of poverty to the tool that addresses it.

questions.prompt: The poverty line prescribed for study is based primarily on:
options: The minimum calorie intake needed per person per day
The average income of the richest region
The price of a standard housing unit
questions.answer: The minimum calorie intake needed per person per day
questions.explanation: The line starts from the physical requirement of energy — roughly 2400 kcal rural and 2100 kcal urban — because below that intake earning capacity itself collapses. Income needed to buy that diet then defines the threshold.
questions.commonMistake: Basing the line on wages or housing alone; those are consequences, while the prescribed basis is calories.

questions.prompt: A family eats adequately and is above the calorie norm, but cannot match the schooling or housing of others in the same town. This is:
questions.explanation: Relative poverty is the distance from others within a society, not a fall below minimum needs. The family meets the absolute standard yet stands far below its neighbours — the second sense the syllabus prescribes.
questions.commonMistake: Calling every hardship absolute poverty — the calorie test is what separates the two senses.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a cause of poverty in the sense the syllabus prescribes?
options: Unequal distribution of the gains from growth
A rise in the general level of literacy
An increase in buffer stock holdings
A fall in the population of working age
questions.answer: Unequal distribution of the gains from growth
questions.explanation: If growth concentrates, national income rises while those at the bottom gain nothing — a cause that reproduces poverty even in a growing economy. The other options reduce poverty rather than cause it.
questions.commonMistake: Reading “cause” as only low income: distribution, population, education and prices are all prescribed mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Why does inflation hurt the poor more than other groups?
options: They spend almost all their income on food, fuel and rent with no cushion
They own the assets whose prices rise
questions.answer: They spend almost all their income on food, fuel and rent with no cushion
questions.explanation: Essentials absorb nearly the entire budget of a poor household, so price rises cut quantity consumed immediately, while richer households’ savings absorb the same rise. The mechanism is budget composition plus absence of savings.
questions.commonMistake: Answering “they buy more” — it is the share of essentials and the missing buffer that matter.

questions.prompt: Complete: the calorie-based poverty line is conventionally drawn at about ________ calories per person per day for a rural area and ________ for an urban area.
questions.explanation: Rural work burns more energy and urban food is more calorie-dense, so the standard convention sets 2400 kcal for rural areas and 2100 for urban — the physical floor beneath earning capacity.
questions.commonMistake: Reversing the pair — the higher norm belongs to rural areas, where manual work is heavier.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the poverty line? State its basis.
questions.answer: The poverty line is the income threshold below which a household cannot meet the basic necessities of life — enough food, clothing, shelter, and access to education and health. Its prescribed basis is calorie intake: a working person needs a minimum daily energy, conventionally about 2400 calories in a rural area and 2100 in an urban one, because falling below that intake weakens the person and reduces earning capacity. The line is then drawn at the income required to buy food delivering that norm together with minimal non-food necessities, and households below it are counted as poor. Because it is built from a physical minimum, the line is absolute: it moves only when the cost of the minimum changes, not when the rich grow richer.
questions.explanation: Full marks need the definition as a threshold, the calorie basis with the physical reasoning, and the note that the line is absolute — the last clause distinguishes a complete answer from a partial one.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the line as “the average income” or a percentage of it — it is a minimum-needs threshold, not an average.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between absolute and relative poverty with an example of each.
questions.answer: Absolute poverty is the condition of falling below the minimum requirements of food and basic necessities — it asks whether a household can meet subsistence at all, and it is measured by the calorie-based poverty line. Example: a landless labourer’s family whose monthly earnings never reach the expenditure needed for the prescribed calorie norm, eating two thin meals a day. Relative poverty is the distance between groups within the same society — it asks how far below others a household stands, and no line measures it because it depends on the comparison group. Example: a worker who eats adequately yet cannot afford the schooling or housing that families in the same town take for granted, or a region left behind while the rest of the country prospers. The two are independent: absolute poverty can fall while relative poverty widens, because raising the floor does not close the gap.
questions.explanation: A full distinction pairs definition, measurement and example on both sides and closes with the independence of the two — that last clause is what shows the senses are not interchangeable.
questions.commonMistake: Calling relative poverty “poverty among the rich” — it is a gap measured within a society, and it can exist below an adequate living standard too.

questions.prompt: Explain any five causes of poverty.
questions.answer: Low income and unemployment come first: where work is casual, seasonal or absent, earnings never rise above the next meal, so no surplus accumulates for education, insurance or assets — the household stays at subsistence because the wage itself does so. Rapid population growth works on the denominator: more members divide the same income, and when young workers enter the labour market faster than jobs are created, unemployment and depressed wages follow — pressure on income and pressure on jobs arrive together. Unequal distribution of income and wealth operates even in a growing economy: if gains concentrate in a few regions, sectors and households, national income rises while the slice reaching the bottom stays the same, so growth alone does not move the count of the poor. Illiteracy and lack of education or training close the loop from the other side: without skills workers are confined to the lowest-paid occupations with no upward route, and their children repeat the confinement because school fees and lost child wages keep education out of reach — poverty passing itself to the next generation. Rising prices complete the set: inflation in food, fuel and rent erodes the real value of fixed and casual incomes, and since the poor spend almost everything on essentials, each price rise reduces the quantity they can buy — earning the same and living worse. The five are mutually reinforcing rather than alternative: unemployment keeps income low, low income blocks education, illiteracy keeps wages low, population pressure widens the low-wage pool, and inflation erodes what the pool earns — which is why isolated remedies fail and causes must be addressed together.
questions.explanation: Five causes with a causal chain each earn full marks; the final paragraph’s showing that the causes interlock converts a list into an explanation and is what a top-band answer adds.
questions.commonMistake: Writing five headings with one clause each — the prescribed “to be discussed” requires the mechanism of every cause stated.

questions.prompt: “A household can be above the poverty line and still be denied development.” Discuss with reference to the two senses of poverty.
questions.answer: The statement holds because the line certifies one thing — the income needed for the calorie minimum — while development requires several things the line does not measure. Take a household just above the threshold: it buys the prescribed diet, so the headcount records it as non-poor, yet its income leaves no margin for a school fee, a clinic visit or a repaired roof. Absolute poverty as measured says nothing about any of those, because the line was built to answer a single question about minimum energy, not a holistic question about capability. The first sense therefore under-counts deprivation by design: it is a floor, and development is about what people can be and do above the floor. The second sense supplies the missing lens. Relative poverty measures distance — the household’s schooling, housing and health stand far below those of families in the same town, so within its society it is positioned low in every dimension that mobility depends on. A child in this household eats adequately yet finishes no schooling, and the gap repeats across generations: relative poverty is not misery, but it is exclusion from the ladder. The mechanisms then explain why the two diverge: distribution concentrates gains so incomes above the line pull away while those just below it barely move; public services that would equalise schooling and health are scarce exactly where the near-poor live; and a shock — illness, job loss, a bad season — can drop a household below the absolute line in a month, showing that the line marks a cliff rather than a slope. Policy follows the diagnosis: food support and wage employment lift households over the absolute floor, while universal education and health, progressive distribution and secure employment address the relative distance that the line is constitutionally blind to. The discussion thus resolves the sentence not as a paradox but as a measurement lesson — poverty lines count deprivation of necessities, development requires freedom and capability, and a country serious about the second must measure what the first was never built to see.
questions.explanation: Discussion marks require the mechanism of blindness (one-question line vs multi-dimensional development), a worked household, the divergence explanation through distribution and services, and paired remedies for the two senses — a bare statement that “lines are imperfect” stays below the band.
questions.commonMistake: Arguing only that the line is set too low — that keeps the debate inside absolute poverty and never engages the relative sense.

questions.prompt: Two neighbours both earn just above the calorie-based line. One saves, the other is wiped out by an illness. Analyse what each case shows about measuring poverty.
questions.answer: Both households are counted identically — non-poor — yet the outcomes diverge completely, and the divergence exposes three properties of the measurement. First, the line records a flow, not a stock: it compares current income with the minimum and stays silent about savings, assets and debt, so a household with a buffer and one with nothing look the same in the year before the shock. The distinction the line misses is resilience, and resilience is exactly what determines whether a bad month ends in a correction or a catastrophe. Second, the shock case shows the poverty of events rather than of income: an illness removes earnings while adding costs, dropping the household below the line instantly — the line measures position at a point in time while poverty for a household is a trajectory with vulnerability built in. Headcount statistics count the catastrophised month but not the thousands of near-line months preceding it, so two economies with identical headcounts can have entirely different exposure. Third, the comparison shows why the relative lens matters even among equals: the household that was wiped out now loses schooling for its children, moving permanently down the mobility ladder while the calorie norm may again be met within a year — absolute measures record recovery, relative measures record the lost generation. The practical conclusion follows for policy design: income supplementation alone treats the symptom shown by the second household only after collapse, while a package of savings access, insurance and health cover addresses the vulnerability that the measurement cannot see — and a reporting system that publishes both the headcount and a near-poor or vulnerable measure gives the programmes their proper target. The examiner’s point, finally, is methodological: a threshold answers one question well and is silent about the rest, and analysis begins where that silence is named rather than hidden.
questions.explanation: The analysis must extract from the pair at least two measurement properties — flow versus stock, point versus trajectory — tie each to a statistical consequence (headcount blindness), and end with the policy and reporting implication; describing the two households without the methodological conclusion stays at comprehension level.
questions.commonMistake: Reading the case as a moral about luck or prudence, which never engages measuring poverty at all.
